subject: GCSE Science
source: Drive: Science Overview sequence and AQA GCSE 9-1 required practical handbooks adapted; AQA 8464 Combined Science Trilogy specification (Organisation; Bonding, structure and properties of matter; Energy), continuing from y10 (cell biology, atomic structure, electricity)

lessons.title: Principles of organisation and the digestive system
objectives: Describe the levels of organisation from cell to organism
Describe the structure and function of the organs of the digestive system
Explain how the digestive system is an example of an organ system

keywords.def: a group of similar cells working together to do a job
a group of different tissues that work together to carry out a function
a group of organs working together to do a job
the organ system that breaks down food and absorbs the products

starter: Bismillah. Name three organelles found in an animal cell.
Define differentiation.
What is the function of mitosis in a multicellular organism?

teach.heading: Levels of organisation
bullets: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism
Specialised cells form tissues
Different tissues form organs
Organs work together in organ systems
teach.note: Link back to Year 10 cell biology: differentiation allows cells to specialise. Example: muscle cells form muscular tissue, which is part of the stomach wall. Ask pupils to place the stomach, glandular tissue, the digestive system and a gastric epithelial cell in order. Qur'an 51:21 invites us to reflect on ourselves: 'And in yourselves, will you not then see?'

teach.heading: Why we digest food
bullets: Food molecules are large and insoluble
They cannot pass through the gut wall
Digestion breaks them into small soluble molecules
Small molecules are absorbed into the blood
teach.note: Ask: why can't a starch molecule get from the gut into the blood? Too big. Digestion is the chemical breakdown of large molecules by enzymes. Contrast with physical breakdown by teeth and stomach churning, which increases surface area for enzymes. Common error: saying that food is 'absorbed' in the stomach.

teach.heading: Organs of the digestive system
bullets: Mouth and salivary glands: amylase starts starch digestion
Stomach: churns food, makes acid and protease
Liver and gall bladder: make and store bile
Pancreas: makes amylase, protease and lipase
teach.note: Use a labelled diagram and trace the path of a piece of bread. Explain that glands are organs that make and release substances. Ask pupils to add each organ to a table: organ, what it makes or does. Mention the stomach's hydrochloric acid at about pH 2 kills microorganisms and provides the optimum pH for its protease.

teach.heading: Small and large intestine
bullets: Small intestine: digestion is completed; soluble food is absorbed
Villi give a large surface area for absorption
Large intestine absorbs water from undigested food
Undigested material leaves as faeces
teach.note: Revisit villi from Year 8. Ask: how is the small intestine adapted for absorption? (long, folded lining with villi, thin walls, rich blood supply). In the large intestine water is absorbed; diarrhoea occurs when this is not done well. Link to Qur'an 7:31, eat and drink but do not be excessive.

teach.heading: Organ system as a whole
bullets: Organs are linked by tubes and blood vessels
The system is controlled and coordinated by the body
Digestion makes small molecules for growth and energy
Failure of one organ affects the whole system
teach.note: Ask pupils: what would happen if the pancreas could not make lipase? (fats not digested; poor absorption). Practise exam-style language: state the function and link structure to function. Pupils should be able to draw the system and annotate three functions.

practice: Name the correct order of levels of organisation.
Where is bile stored?
State one function of the large intestine.
independent: Draw and label the digestive system with a function for each of eight parts.
Explain why large food molecules must be digested before absorption. (3 marks)
The stomach is made of muscular tissue, glandular tissue and epithelial tissue. Explain why it is an organ. (2 marks)
Describe how the small intestine is adapted for absorption. (3 marks)
exit: Define organ system.
Name two organs that make digestive enzymes.
lessons.homework: Draw a flow chart showing the pathway of a cheese sandwich through the digestive system, naming each organ and what happens to the food there.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled outline with a word bank. EAL: pre-teach 'gland' and 'absorb' with pictures. Stretch: explain why a person who has had their gall bladder removed may need to eat less fatty food.

lessons.title: Enzymes and the effect of pH
objectives: Describe how enzymes work using the lock and key model
Explain the effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity
Plan and analyse the amylase and pH required practical

keywords.def: a biological catalyst that speeds up a reaction without being used up
the part of an enzyme where the substrate binds
an enzyme whose shape has changed so the active site no longer fits
the temperature or pH at which an enzyme works best

starter: Which organs produce digestive enzymes?
Why must food be digested before it can be absorbed?
Define catalyst.

teach.heading: Enzymes as biological catalysts
bullets: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions
Not used up in the reaction
Each enzyme works on one substrate
Digestive enzymes work in the gut
teach.note: Revise catalysts from the chemistry course (substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up). Stress that enzymes are catalysts made by living cells. They are specific. Ask pupils why we need enzymes: reactions would be too slow at body temperature.

teach.heading: Lock and key model
bullets: Substrate fits into the active site
An enzyme-substrate complex forms
Products are released and the enzyme is reused
The shape of the active site is specific
teach.note: Draw the model in three stages: substrate, complex, products. Introduce the term complementary shape. Note that the lock and key model has been refined, but AQA requires the lock and key model. Ask: what would happen if a different molecule entered the active site? It would not fit.

teach.heading: Temperature and pH
bullets: Rate increases with temperature up to an optimum
Too hot: the active site changes shape
Enzymes are denatured at high temperature or extreme pH
Different enzymes have different optimum pH
teach.note: Sketch rate against temperature and rate against pH on the board. Human enzymes usually have an optimum at about 37°C. Stomach protease works best at about pH 2; amylase from the pancreas at about pH 7-8. Misconception: enzymes are killed. They are not alive; they are denatured. Denaturation is irreversible.

teach.heading: Required practical: amylase and pH
bullets: Mix starch, buffer solution and amylase
Take samples every 30 s into iodine on a spotting tile
Time taken until iodine stays orange-brown
Repeat at several pH values; keep temperature at 35-40°C
teach.note: Set out the method: place drops of iodine in wells, add starch solution, buffer and amylase to a tube in a water bath, remove a drop every 30 s. When iodine no longer turns blue-black, starch has gone. Variables: independent pH, dependent time (or rate = 1000 ÷ time), controlled temperature, volumes and concentrations. Safety: iodine stains and is an irritant.

teach.heading: Analysing results
bullets: Rate = 1000 ÷ time in seconds
Plot rate against pH
Optimum is the peak of the curve
Use repeats and means to improve reliability
teach.note: Data: pH 4, 300 s; pH 6, 90 s; pH 7, 60 s; pH 8, 120 s; pH 10, no change after 600 s. Rates are 3.3, 11.1, 16.7, 8.3 and 1.7. Optimum is around pH 7. Ask: how could we find the optimum more precisely? Use smaller pH steps near 7. Evaluate: judging the end point is subjective.

practice: What type of molecule is an enzyme?
What does denatured mean?
Name the substrate of amylase.
independent: Draw the lock and key model for an enzyme with labels.
Explain why boiling an enzyme stops it working. (3 marks)
Use the data set in the lesson to calculate the rate for each pH and plot a graph.
Describe how the pancreatic amylase and stomach protease are adapted to their pH conditions. (2 marks)
exit: State how pH affects the rate of enzyme activity.
Why is a water bath used in the amylase practical?
lessons.homework: Write a method paragraph for the amylase and pH required practical, including variables and one safety precaution.
lessons.send: SEND: step-by-step method card and data table template. EAL: pre-teach 'substrate', 'complex' and 'optimum'. Stretch: explain why enzyme rate stops increasing even at a high substrate concentration.

lessons.title: Digestive enzymes, bile and food tests
objectives: State the substrate, product and site of production of amylase, protease and lipase
Explain the role of bile in digestion
Describe the tests for sugars, starch, protein and lipids

keywords.def: an enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates
breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones to increase surface area
an alkaline liquid made in the liver that helps digest fats
a sugar that gives a positive result with Benedict's solution

starter: What does denatured mean?
Name the organ that makes bile.
State the optimum temperature of human enzymes.

teach.heading: Digestive enzymes
bullets: Amylase: starch → maltose (sugars)
Protease: proteins → amino acids
Lipase: lipids (fats) → glycerol and fatty acids
Amylase and protease are made in several organs
teach.note: Make a table: enzyme, substrate, products, where made. Amylase: salivary glands, pancreas, small intestine. Protease: stomach, pancreas, small intestine. Lipase: pancreas, small intestine. Say that maltose is broken down further into glucose by other carbohydrases. Misconception: amylase works only in the mouth.

teach.heading: What happens to the products?
bullets: Small molecules are absorbed into the blood
Used to build new carbohydrates, proteins and lipids
Some glucose is used in respiration
Amino acids make new proteins for growth and repair
teach.note: Link this to Year 10 cell biology and to nutrition. Ask: where do your muscles get new protein from? Digested amino acids from food. Reinforce that digestion produces building blocks for the body as well as fuel.

teach.heading: Bile
bullets: Made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder
Alkaline: neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach
Gives the right pH for enzymes in the small intestine
Emulsifies fat to give a larger surface area for lipase
teach.note: Draw a large fat droplet broken into many small droplets. Ask: why does a bigger surface area speed up digestion? More contact with lipase. Misconception: bile is an enzyme. It is not; it does not chemically break down fat. Ask pupils: why does the small intestine need an alkaline condition?

teach.heading: Required practical: food tests
bullets: Starch: iodine solution turns blue-black
Sugar: Benedict's solution, heat, green to brick red
Protein: biuret reagent turns purple
Lipids: Sudan III stains the fat layer red
teach.note: Pupils should know the method: grind food with distilled water, filter, then test. Benedict's needs warming in a water bath at about 75°C. Safety: biuret contains copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide: corrosive; wear eye protection. Show a video of each test; the brown paper test for fat can be done at home as a simple alternative.

teach.heading: Interpreting results
bullets: Positive/negative results depend on a colour change
Colour scale shows the amount of sugar: blue, green, yellow, orange, brick red
Use a control with water to compare
Results: potato gives a positive starch test
teach.note: Show a table of foods and results. Ask pupils to identify which food contains protein and starch. Discuss why we use water as a negative control. Link to exam style: 'Describe how you would test a food sample for the presence of protein.' Marks for: sample prepared in solution, add biuret, observe purple.

practice: State the products of protease digestion.
Where is bile stored?
What colour does iodine turn in the presence of starch?
independent: Complete a table for amylase, protease and lipase: substrate, product, where made.
Explain two ways in which bile helps digestion. (4 marks)
A food gives a blue colour with Benedict's, a blue-black with iodine and a purple colour with biuret. State what the food contains.
Describe how to test a food for reducing sugars. (4 marks)
exit: Why does emulsification speed up fat digestion?
What colour does a positive biuret test give?
lessons.homework: Write a 'how to' sheet for the food tests, including expected colours for positive and negative results.
lessons.send: SEND: table template and colour-coded cards for the tests. EAL: key terms with images; reinforce 'positive' and 'negative'. Stretch: design a fair set of controls for the food tests, explaining why a water sample is included.

lessons.title: The heart, lungs and double circulation
objectives: Describe the structure and function of the heart and its blood vessels
Explain what is meant by a double circulatory system
Explain how the lungs are adapted for gas exchange

keywords.def: a system in which blood passes through the heart twice on each circuit
an upper chamber of the heart that receives blood
a lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out
a group of cells in the right atrium that controls the resting heart rate

starter: Name the organ system that digests food.
Which enzyme digests lipids?
State the function of bile.

teach.heading: Structure of the heart
bullets: Four chambers: right and left atria and ventricles
Valves prevent backflow of blood
Septum separates the left and right sides
Muscular walls; left ventricle wall is thickest
teach.note: Draw the heart from the pupil's point of view (as it appears in the body: left side on their right). Label vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, aorta and coronary arteries. Ask why the left ventricle has a thicker wall: it pumps blood around the whole body at higher pressure.

teach.heading: Path of the blood
bullets: Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle
Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs
Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle
Left ventricle → aorta → body
teach.note: Trace the route with arrows: ask pupils to describe the journey of a red blood cell from the foot to the lungs and back. Blood in the right side is deoxygenated; blood in the left side is oxygenated. Misconception: veins always carry deoxygenated blood. The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

teach.heading: Double circulatory system
bullets: Circuit 1: heart to lungs and back
Circuit 2: heart to the body and back
Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit
Gives high pressure to the body and efficient gas exchange
teach.note: Explain that the lungs' capillaries are delicate, so blood is pumped at a lower pressure; after returning to the heart it is boosted to higher pressure for the body. Ask: what would happen if there were a single circuit? Pressure would fall after the lungs. Link to the energy needs of warm-blooded animals.

teach.heading: Controlling the heart
bullets: Natural pacemaker cells in the right atrium
They control the resting heart rate
Artificial pacemakers correct irregular heartbeat
Heart rate increases during exercise
teach.note: Introduce the pacemaker as an example of an electrical signal controlling muscle contraction. Ask: who might need an artificial pacemaker? Those whose natural pacemaker does not work properly. Link to exercise from KS3: more oxygen needed for respiration.

teach.heading: The lungs and gas exchange
bullets: Lungs are in the thorax, protected by the ribs
Alveoli: large surface area, thin walls, rich blood supply
Oxygen diffuses into the blood; carbon dioxide diffuses out
Ventilation maintains the concentration gradient
teach.note: Revise Year 9 gas exchange at GCSE depth with correct language: diffusion down a concentration gradient. Explain the roles of the capillary network and the moist lining. Use 'compare' marks: ask pupils to compare alveoli and villi (both have large surface area, thin walls and good blood supply).

practice: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the lungs.
Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right?
What is the function of valves in the heart?
independent: Draw a labelled diagram of the heart and show the pathway of blood.
Explain why humans have a double circulatory system. (3 marks)
Explain how the structure of alveoli allows efficient gas exchange. (4 marks)
The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. Explain why this is not a contradiction of 'veins carry blood towards the heart'. (2 marks)
exit: Which chamber pumps blood to the body?
What does the natural pacemaker do?
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled double circulation diagram using two colours for oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded outline of the heart. EAL: pre-teach 'atrium', 'ventricle' using a pictorial glossary. Stretch: explain why a hole in the septum would reduce the efficiency of a double circulation.

lessons.title: Blood vessels and blood
objectives: Compare the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries
Calculate blood flow rate
Describe the components of blood and their functions

keywords.def: a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure
a blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart
a tiny blood vessel where exchange takes place with cells
a red protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen

starter: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
Name the blood vessel that leaves the left ventricle.
Where does gas exchange occur in the lungs?

teach.heading: Arteries
bullets: Carry blood away from the heart
Thick, muscular, elastic walls
Narrow lumen
Carry blood at high pressure
teach.note: Show cross-sections. Ask: why do arteries need thick walls? To withstand high pressure and stretch/recoil with each heartbeat. You can feel your pulse in an artery (radial or carotid). Misconception: arteries always carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery does not).

teach.heading: Veins and capillaries
bullets: Veins: thinner walls, large lumen, valves
Valves stop blood flowing backwards
Capillaries: one cell thick, permeable walls
Capillaries allow substances to diffuse into and out of cells
teach.note: Compare in a table: wall thickness, lumen size, valves, pressure. Ask why veins do not need thick walls: the pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; thin walls give a short diffusion distance. Ask pupils about veins in the legs: muscle contractions help push blood back to the heart.

teach.heading: Blood flow rate
bullets: Rate = volume of blood ÷ time
Units: cm³/min
Example: 300 cm³ in 5 minutes = 60 cm³/min
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (extension)
teach.note: Maths skill. Another example: 4500 cm³ per minute for an adult at rest. Ask: how many cm³ in 10 minutes? 45 000. Rearrange: volume = rate × time. Emphasise units. Cardiac output is not on the Trilogy spec; use only for stretch.

teach.heading: Components of blood
bullets: Plasma: carries CO₂, digested food, urea and hormones
Red blood cells carry oxygen
White blood cells defend against pathogens
Platelets help blood to clot
teach.note: Show a micrograph. Ask pupils to say which part is liquid (plasma) and which are cells or fragments. Platelets are fragments of cells. Link to defences against pathogens in the infection topic. Misconception: blood is red because of plasma; plasma is straw coloured.

teach.heading: Blood cells in detail
bullets: Red blood cells: biconcave disc, no nucleus, contain haemoglobin
Haemoglobin + oxygen → oxyhaemoglobin
White blood cells: phagocytes engulf; lymphocytes make antibodies
Platelets: form clots and scabs
teach.note: Ask pupils to link structure to function. Biconcave shape gives a larger surface area for oxygen absorption; lack of nucleus gives more space for haemoglobin. Draw the oxygen binding in lungs and release in tissues. White blood cells are covered in more detail in the Infection and response topic.

practice: Name the blood vessels that have valves.
What is the function of platelets?
Calculate the flow rate if 600 cm³ passes in 4 min.
independent: Complete a table comparing arteries, veins and capillaries: wall, lumen, valves, pressure, function.
Explain how red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen. (3 marks)
Calculate the volume of blood flowing in 15 minutes at 70 cm³/min.
Compare the functions of plasma and platelets. (2 marks)
exit: Why do veins have valves?
State two functions of plasma.
lessons.homework: Create a revision poster summarising the three blood vessels and four components of blood.
lessons.send: SEND: comparison table with prompts. EAL: key term cards with diagrams. Stretch: explain why a capillary network is needed around every cell.

lessons.title: Coronary heart disease and treatments
objectives: Describe how coronary heart disease develops
Evaluate treatments: statins, stents, valves, transplants and artificial hearts
Explain the risk factors that increase the chance of CHD

keywords.def: a condition where fatty deposits narrow the coronary arteries
a tube placed inside an artery to keep it open
a drug that reduces blood cholesterol levels
a fatty substance in the blood that can build up in arteries

starter: Name the blood vessels supplying the heart muscle.
State the function of the valves in the heart.
Which blood vessel carries blood at the highest pressure?

teach.heading: Coronary heart disease (CHD)
bullets: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with oxygen
Fatty material builds up in the arteries
The lumen narrows and blood flow is reduced
Less oxygen reaches the heart muscle, which can cause a heart attack
teach.note: Draw a cross-section of a healthy artery and a narrowed one. Ask: what does the heart muscle need from the blood? Oxygen and glucose for respiration. Explain that a total blockage causes a heart attack. Mention that in the UK CHD is among the leading causes of death.

teach.heading: Risk factors
bullets: Diet high in saturated fat
Smoking
High blood pressure and lack of exercise
Genetic factors and age
teach.note: Link to lifestyle and non-communicable disease. Revisit Year 9 on smoking. Ask: how might smoking increase the risk of CHD? It damages the artery lining and raises blood pressure. Say that risk factors are correlated with disease; they are not guaranteed causes for an individual. Qur'an 2:195 and 7:31 as a link to caring for the body.

teach.heading: Stents and statins
bullets: Stent: a mesh tube keeps the coronary artery open
Quick recovery; but risk of blood clots
Statins reduce blood cholesterol
Long-term treatment; possible side effects such as muscle pain
teach.note: Evaluate: stents give immediate relief but do not tackle the cause; statins slow fatty deposits but need to be taken for life and can have side effects. Present the benefits and risks in a table. Ask: who might choose a stent rather than a statin? Someone with a blocked artery needing quick treatment.

teach.heading: Heart valves and heart failure
bullets: Valves may leak or become stiff
Replace with biological valves (animal or human) or mechanical valves
Heart failure: transplant from a donor, or an artificial heart
Artificial hearts are temporary while waiting for a donor
teach.note: Ask pupils to compare biological and mechanical valves: biological valves do not need long-term blood-thinning drugs but may wear out; mechanical valves last longer but need drugs to prevent clots. Discuss the shortage of donor hearts and rejection by the immune system. Remind pupils of the Islamic view on the importance of preserving life; avoid detailed jurisprudence on organ donation and refer pupils to qualified scholars if they ask.

teach.heading: Evaluating treatments
bullets: Consider effectiveness, risk, cost and recovery
Prevention is better than cure
Lifestyle: healthy diet, exercise, no smoking
Medical treatments are used when lifestyle is not enough
teach.note: Practise 6-mark evaluation answers with a structure: describe each treatment, give advantages, give disadvantages, reach a judgement. Provide a case: a 55-year-old with narrowed arteries. Ask pupils to advise. Stress balanced answers and a conclusion that links to the case.

practice: What substance builds up in the coronary arteries?
Give two risk factors for CHD.
What is the job of a stent?
independent: Explain how fatty deposits in coronary arteries can lead to a heart attack. (4 marks)
Compare statins and stents as treatments for CHD. (4 marks)
Evaluate the use of mechanical and biological heart valves. (4 marks)
A patient has severe heart failure. Suggest and justify two possible treatments. (4 marks)
exit: How does a statin reduce the risk of CHD?
Give one disadvantage of an artificial heart.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Evaluate treatments for coronary heart disease.' Use a table to plan.
lessons.send: SEND: evaluation frame (advantage, disadvantage, conclusion). EAL: glossary for 'stent' and 'valve'. Stretch: explain why statins are given to some people who do not yet have symptoms.

lessons.title: Non-communicable disease, risk factors and cancer
objectives: Distinguish communicable from non-communicable diseases
Explain how lifestyle, genes and the environment are risk factors
Describe cancer, benign and malignant tumours and cancer risk factors

keywords.def: a disease that cannot be passed from person to person
something that increases the chance of a person getting a disease
a growth of abnormal cells that stays in one place
cancer cells that invade neighbouring tissues and spread in the blood

starter: Name two risk factors for coronary heart disease.
What is mitosis?
Define a pathogen.

teach.heading: Health and disease
bullets: Health is physical and mental wellbeing
Diseases may be communicable or non-communicable
Communicable: caused by pathogens, e.g. flu
Non-communicable: e.g. cancer, CHD, type 2 diabetes
teach.note: Ask pupils for examples of each type. Discuss interactions: defects in the immune system can lead to more infections; viruses can trigger cancers (e.g. HPV); immune reactions can cause allergies such as asthma; severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness. Stress that mental health is part of health.

teach.heading: Risk factors
bullets: Lifestyle: diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol
Obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes
Smoking is a risk factor for lung disease and cancer
Alcohol affects the liver and brain; also a risk to unborn babies
teach.note: Be sensitive. Alcohol is haram: use the biology (liver, brain, unborn baby) to show the wisdom of the prohibition without discussing drinking in detail. Qur'an 5:90 tells believers to avoid intoxicants. Smoking and obesity examples link to the diet and exercise discussion.

teach.heading: Correlation and causation
bullets: Correlation: two variables change together
Causation: a change in one causes a change in the other
Studies show smoking correlated with lung cancer, and many mechanisms are known
Data must be from large samples and be repeated
teach.note: Show a graph of cigarette consumption and lung cancer rate. Ask: does correlation prove causation? No, but evidence from mechanisms (carcinogens in smoke) and many studies supports a causal link. Provide a counterexample: ice-cream sales and sunburn. Evaluate studies by sample size and control of variables.

teach.heading: Cancer
bullets: Cancer is uncontrolled cell division
A tumour is a mass of abnormal cells
Benign: stays in one place in a membrane; not cancer
Malignant: invades other tissues and spreads in the blood
teach.note: Link to the cell cycle and mitosis from Year 10. Explain that tumours can be benign or malignant. Secondary tumours form when malignant cells spread. Ask: why are malignant tumours more dangerous? They spread and are harder to treat. Misconception: all lumps are cancer.

teach.heading: Cancer risk factors and the cost of disease
bullets: Smoking, obesity, UV radiation, viruses, ionising radiation
Some genetic risk factors, e.g. certain inherited genes
Costs: human suffering and financial cost to the NHS
Prevention: healthy lifestyle and screening
teach.note: Discuss that scientists have identified lifestyle risk factors and genetic ones such as BRCA genes. Ask pupils: what are the costs of non-communicable diseases for families and society? Lost work, treatment costs, loss of life. Reinforce the idea of prevention as a trust to our bodies. Finish with a short reflection on gratitude for health (shukr).

practice: Give one example of a communicable disease.
Which type of tumour spreads to other parts of the body?
State two lifestyle risk factors for type 2 diabetes.
independent: Sort ten diseases into communicable and non-communicable.
Explain the difference between benign and malignant tumours. (3 marks)
A study shows people who eat more processed meat have a higher rate of bowel cancer. Explain why this does not prove that processed meat causes cancer. (3 marks)
Discuss the costs of non-communicable diseases to individuals and to society. (4 marks)
exit: Define risk factor.
Why can malignant tumours be life-threatening?
lessons.homework: Research one non-communicable disease and write a fact sheet with causes, risk factors and prevention.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards and a graph-reading frame. EAL: key terms with picture cards. Stretch: evaluate a data set showing smoking and lung cancer rates over 50 years.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: Ionic bonding
objectives: Describe how ionic bonds form by the transfer of electrons
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for simple ionic compounds
Work out the charge on ions from the group and write ionic formulae

keywords.def: a charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons
the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
a positively charged ion
a negatively charged ion

starter: Bismillah. Write the electronic structure of sodium (atomic number 11).
In which group is chlorine and how many outer electrons does it have?
Explain why noble gases are unreactive.

teach.heading: Atoms into ions
bullets: Atoms are neutral: protons equal electrons
Atoms lose or gain electrons to get a full outer shell
Losing electrons gives a positive ion
Gaining electrons gives a negative ion
teach.note: Recall electronic structures from Year 10. Use sodium (2,8,1) and chlorine (2,8,7). Sodium loses one electron to become Na⁺ (2,8); chlorine gains one to become Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Both have the stable structure of a noble gas. Misconception: ions are 'bigger atoms'. Stress the change in number of electrons, not protons.

teach.heading: Ionic bonding
bullets: Metal atoms transfer electrons to non-metal atoms
Opposite charges attract strongly
This electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond
Example: sodium chloride, NaCl
teach.note: Draw the transfer with an arrow from sodium to chlorine. Ask: why do metals form positive ions and non-metals negative ions? Metals have few outer electrons and lose them easily.

teach.heading: Charges of ions
bullets: Group 1: +1; Group 2: +2
Group 6: −2; Group 7: −1
Group 3 forms 3+ ions; Group 5 forms 3− ions
Charge matches the electrons lost or gained
teach.note: Make a table with sodium Na⁺, magnesium Mg²⁺, aluminium Al³⁺, oxygen O²⁻, chlorine Cl⁻, nitrogen N³⁻. Ask pupils to predict the charge on lithium and sulfur. Transition metals can form more than one ion (for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺); the charge is given in the name, as in iron(III).

teach.heading: Dot-and-cross diagrams
bullets: Show only outer shells
Use dots for one atom and crosses for the other
Square brackets with the charge
Example: MgO is Mg²⁺ and O²⁻
teach.note: Model magnesium oxide: Mg gives two electrons to O; show Mg²⁺ with no outer shell visible (2,8) and O²⁻ with 8 electrons in outer shell. Another: sodium chloride. Insist on square brackets and charges. Common mistake: showing electron arrows but leaving charges off, or drawing the wrong number of electrons on the anion.

teach.heading: Working out formulae
bullets: Compound must have no overall charge
Balance the + and − charges
Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻: need two Cl⁻, so MgCl₂
Al³⁺ and O²⁻: Al₂O₃
teach.note: Use the 'criss-cross' method with understanding. For MgCl2: +2 balanced by 2 × −1. For Al2O3: 2 × +3 = +6, 3 × −2 = −6. Practise with sodium oxide (Na2O), calcium fluoride (CaF2), potassium bromide (KBr). Ask: why does sodium chloride have the formula NaCl and not NaCl2?

practice: Write the ion formed when magnesium loses two electrons.
What type of elements form positive ions?
Draw the electronic structure of a chloride ion.
independent: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for NaCl and MgO.
Give the formula and charges for: calcium chloride, lithium oxide, aluminium chloride.
Explain why Group 7 elements form 1− ions and Group 2 elements form 2+ ions. (4 marks)
Describe what happens to the electrons when potassium reacts with bromine. (3 marks)
exit: Define ionic bond.
State the formula of magnesium chloride and explain why.
lessons.homework: Complete a table of ten ionic compounds: name, ions with charges, formula.
lessons.send: SEND: periodic table with group charges highlighted; templates for dot-and-cross. EAL: glossary 'transfer', 'attract'. Stretch: work out the formula of aluminium sulfide and explain the charges.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: Properties of ionic compounds
objectives: Describe the giant ionic lattice structure
Explain the properties of ionic compounds: melting point and electrical conductivity
Evaluate the different models used to represent ionic compounds

keywords.def: a regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces
a force of attraction between opposite charges
melted; in the liquid state
a substance that allows electricity to flow through it

starter: Write the formula of magnesium oxide and name the ions.
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride.
State the charges on the ions in calcium chloride.

teach.heading: The giant ionic lattice
bullets: Ions are arranged in a regular repeating pattern
Each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions
Strong electrostatic forces act in all directions
Sodium chloride forms cubic crystals
teach.note: Show a 3D model of sodium chloride (or a ball-and-stick animation). Draw the 2D diagram with alternating + and − ions. Ask: why does NaCl have a regular shape when you look at table salt crystals under a magnifier? Because of the regular lattice. A single formula unit does not exist as a molecule.

teach.heading: Melting and boiling points
bullets: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points
Strong forces between ions need lots of energy to overcome
Sodium chloride melts at about 801°C
Solid at room temperature
teach.note: Compare data: NaCl 801°C, MgO 2852°C. Ask why MgO has a higher melting point (larger charges, stronger attraction). Misconception: covalent bonds break when melting an ionic compound. In ionic compounds the lattice is broken apart as ions move more freely.

teach.heading: Conducting electricity
bullets: Solid: ions are fixed in position; cannot conduct
Molten: ions are free to move and carry charge
Dissolved in water: ions are free to move
Conducts only when molten or in solution
teach.note: Explain why electricity is carried by moving charged particles: in metals electrons, in ionic liquids ions. Show video of salt solution lighting a bulb. Ask: why doesn't solid salt conduct? Ions locked in place. Remind pupils that pure water is a poor conductor; salt water conducts.

teach.heading: Solubility and strength
bullets: Many ionic compounds dissolve in water
Brittle: a blow shifts ions so like charges repel
Crystals shatter along flat planes
Hard but brittle
teach.note: Illustrate the brittle property with a diagram of rows of ions sliding by one position: like charges meet and repel. Ask: why can't you bend a salt crystal like a metal wire? Because repulsion splits the crystal. Note: not all ionic compounds are soluble (e.g. barium sulfate), so don't over-generalise.

teach.heading: Models of ionic compounds
bullets: Dot-and-cross: shows electrons but not the lattice
2D lattice: shows arrangement but not 3D
Ball-and-stick: shows 3D but ions look like they have gaps
3D space-filling: more realistic but hard to see inside
teach.note: Ask pupils to evaluate each model. For example the dot-and-cross shows only one pair of ions; 2D diagrams show only one layer; ball and stick suggests that bonds are sticks. Practise the AQA skill of using the models to give advantages and limitations. Link to the idea that scientific models are improved over time.

practice: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
Does solid sodium chloride conduct electricity? Explain.
Name the type of force between ions.
independent: Complete a table: property, observation, explanation, for ionic compounds.
Explain why molten sodium chloride conducts electricity but solid sodium chloride does not. (4 marks)
Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. (3 marks)
Evaluate the ball-and-stick model of sodium chloride. (3 marks)
exit: State two properties of ionic compounds.
Why are ionic crystals brittle?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph for the question: 'Explain the properties of sodium chloride in terms of its structure and bonding.'
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters for explaining conduction. EAL: pre-teach 'lattice', 'brittle', 'molten'. Stretch: explain using ion charges and sizes why MgO melts at a much higher temperature than NaCl.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: States of matter and changes of state
objectives: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases
Name the changes of state and explain them in terms of energy
Use state symbols and evaluate the particle model

keywords.def: the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid
the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas
a solid changing directly to a gas
(s), (l), (g) or (aq) after a formula showing the state of a substance

starter: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
Define a compound.
Name the three states of matter.

teach.heading: Particle model
bullets: Solid: particles close, regular pattern, vibrate
Liquid: close, irregular, move past each other
Gas: far apart, random, move quickly
Particles are held by forces of attraction
teach.note: Draw each state with arrows for movement. Link to the Year 7 and 8 particle model. Ask pupils to explain why gases are compressible but liquids are not. In a gas, there are large gaps. Misconception: particles in solids do not move; they vibrate about fixed positions.

teach.heading: Changes of state
bullets: Melting and freezing
Boiling (evaporating) and condensing
Sublimation (solid to gas) and deposition
Physical changes: no new substances
teach.note: Draw the cycle with the labels and ask pupils to give an example of each. Sublimation: dry ice or iodine. Emphasise that changes of state are physical changes, they are reversible, and the mass is conserved. The particles are the same before and after.

teach.heading: Energy and changes of state
bullets: Heating gives particles more energy
At melting point, energy overcomes forces between particles
The stronger the forces, the higher the melting point
Temperature stays constant during a change of state
teach.note: Show a heating curve for water or sketch one. Explain that the flat sections are when the added energy is used to break attractions, not to raise temperature. Ask: what happens to the energy during boiling? It overcomes forces to separate particles.

teach.heading: Predicting state
bullets: Below melting point: solid
Between melting and boiling point: liquid
Above boiling point: gas
Example: oxygen m.p. −219°C, b.p. −183°C; at −200°C it is a liquid
teach.note: Provide data: ethanol m.p. −114°C, b.p. 78°C; chlorine m.p. −101°C, b.p. −34°C; sodium chloride m.p. 801°C. Pupils determine the state at 20°C. Also note that state at room temperature is about 20°C. Practise reading data tables and decimals with negatives.

teach.heading: State symbols and limitations
bullets: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution
Example: NaCl(s) → NaCl(aq) on dissolving
Particle model treats particles as spheres
It ignores forces between particles and gaps in the model
teach.note: State symbols are used in equations, for example 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s). Aqueous means dissolved in water. Ask pupils to evaluate the particle model: it explains pressure, density and diffusion but it shows particles as solid spheres and does not show forces or the real sizes of particles.

practice: Name the change of state from liquid to gas.
In which state are particles furthest apart?
What does (aq) mean?
independent: Draw particle diagrams of a solid, liquid and gas, each with 12 particles.
State whether each is solid, liquid or gas at 25°C: m.p./b.p. data given for five substances.
Explain why the temperature stays constant while ice melts. (3 marks)
Write a balanced equation with state symbols for sodium reacting with chlorine.
exit: Describe the movement of particles in a liquid.
What is meant by sublimation?
lessons.homework: Create a flow chart of the changes of state, with an example and an energy change for each.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn particle boxes to fill in. EAL: pre-teach 'vibrate' and 'attraction' with actions. Stretch: sketch and explain a heating curve for a substance as it goes from solid to gas.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: Covalent bonding and small molecules
objectives: Describe a covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for simple molecules
Explain the properties of simple molecular substances

keywords.def: a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms
a group of atoms joined by covalent bonds
a weak force of attraction between molecules
a very large molecule made of many repeating units

starter: Define ionic bond.
State the difference between an element and a compound.
Which elements form covalent bonds?

teach.heading: Sharing electrons
bullets: Non-metal atoms share electrons
Each shared pair is one covalent bond
Atoms gain a full outer shell
Covalent bonds are strong
teach.note: Contrast with ionic: transfer vs sharing. Draw hydrogen H₂: two atoms each with one electron share a pair, giving each a full first shell. Ask: why do metals not form covalent molecules? They lose electrons easily. Misconception: covalent bonds are weak. The bonds within a molecule are strong; the forces between molecules are weak.

teach.heading: Dot-and-cross diagrams
bullets: H₂, Cl₂, HCl, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, CO₂, O₂
Show only the outer electrons
Overlap circles at the shared pair
Double bond in O₂ and CO₂
teach.note: Draw HCl, H2O and CH4 step by step. Count outer electrons: C has 4, each H has 1; four shared pairs. For O2 and CO2 there are double bonds (two shared pairs). Practise drawing methane, ammonia and water with all outer electrons, including lone pairs. Ask pupils to check each atom has a full outer shell.

teach.heading: Displayed formulae
bullets: A line represents a shared pair
H–H, H–Cl, O=O, O=C=O
Displayed formulae show the bonds but not the electrons
Molecular formula: how many of each atom
teach.note: Pupils convert dot-and-cross to displayed formulae and back. Show ethane, methane. Ask: what are the limitations of a displayed formula? It does not show 3D shape or the lone pairs. Revisit the structure of simple alkanes and alcohols in organic chemistry later.

teach.heading: Properties of small molecules
bullets: Low melting and boiling points
Weak intermolecular forces are overcome, not covalent bonds
Do not conduct electricity: no free charged particles
Usually gases or liquids at room temperature
teach.note: Common misconception: covalent bonds break when a molecular substance melts or boils. Draw water boiling: H2O molecules separate, but each molecule stays H2O. Ask: why can't molecular substances conduct? No ions or free electrons. Compare with ionic compounds.

teach.heading: Bigger molecules and polymers
bullets: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces
Boiling points rise as molecules get bigger
Polymers have very long chains of repeating units
Polymers are usually solid at room temperature
teach.note: Provide data for methane, ethane, propane, butane, showing a rise in boiling point. Explain that more electrons and atoms give stronger forces. Show a repeat unit for poly(ethene) with a bracket and n. Poly(ethene) is a solid because the intermolecular forces between long chains are strong.

practice: How many electrons are shared in a double bond?
Why do simple molecular substances have low boiling points?
Draw the displayed formula of water.
independent: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for HCl, H₂O, NH₃ and CH₄.
Explain why methane has a low boiling point. (3 marks)
Explain why molecular substances do not conduct electricity. (2 marks)
The boiling points of ethane and decane are −89°C and 174°C. Explain the difference. (3 marks)
exit: Define covalent bond.
Which forces are overcome when water boils?
lessons.homework: Complete a table of five molecules with formula, dot-and-cross diagram and displayed formula.
lessons.send: SEND: outline circles for dot-and-cross diagrams. EAL: pre-teach 'share' and 'molecule'. Stretch: draw the dot-and-cross diagram for ethene (C₂H₄) and identify the double bond.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: Giant covalent structures: diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide
objectives: Describe giant covalent structures
Explain the properties of diamond and graphite in terms of bonding
State the structure and properties of silicon dioxide

keywords.def: a huge network of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
a different structural form of the same element
an electron that is free to move through a structure
with six sides

starter: Why do small molecules have low melting points?
Define covalent bond.
Draw the displayed formula of methane.

teach.heading: Giant covalent structures
bullets: Billions of atoms joined by covalent bonds
Regular lattice with no separate molecules
Very high melting and boiling points
Examples: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide
teach.note: Contrast with small molecules. Ask: what must be broken to melt diamond? Many strong covalent bonds. Not weak intermolecular forces. Show 3D models if possible. Pupils should not call these 'giant ionic'; there are no ions.

teach.heading: Diamond
bullets: Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds
Rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice
Very hard; very high melting point
Does not conduct: no free electrons
teach.note: Uses: cutting tools, drill bits, jewellery. Link property to structure: four strong bonds per atom, so very hard. Ask: why does diamond not conduct? All four outer electrons are used in bonding. Misconception: diamond is a different element from carbon.

teach.heading: Graphite
bullets: Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds
Layers of hexagonal rings
Weak forces between layers
One delocalised electron per carbon atom
teach.note: Draw a layer of hexagons with the spare electron delocalised. Ask: why is graphite soft and slippery? Layers slide over each other because the forces between layers are weak. Why does graphite conduct electricity? Delocalised electrons can move along layers. Graphite has a high melting point because of the strong covalent bonds within layers.

teach.heading: Silicon dioxide
bullets: Silicon dioxide, SiO₂, is the main part of sand
Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms
Each oxygen atom bonded to two silicon atoms
Structure like diamond: hard, high melting point
teach.note: The formula SiO2 shows the ratio of atoms, not a molecule. Melting point about 1700°C. Ask: why does silicon dioxide not conduct? No free electrons or ions. Uses: glass making, building materials. Link to the efficient use of sand, an Earth resource.

teach.heading: Comparing the structures
bullets: Diamond: hard, insulator
Graphite: soft, conductor
Silicon dioxide: hard, insulator
All have high melting points from many strong covalent bonds
teach.note: Complete a comparison table on the board. Pupils practise 'explain' answers with three parts: observation, structure, reason. For example, 'Graphite conducts because each carbon forms only three bonds, so one electron per atom is delocalised and free to carry charge.'

practice: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in diamond?
Why does graphite conduct electricity?
Name the substance which is the main component of sand.
independent: Make a table comparing diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide: bonding, structure, hardness, conductivity, uses.
Explain why diamond has a very high melting point. (3 marks)
Explain why graphite is used as a lubricant and as electrodes. (4 marks)
Silicon dioxide and carbon dioxide are both oxides of Group 4 elements. Explain why SiO₂ is a solid but CO₂ is a gas at room temperature. (4 marks)
exit: Describe the structure of graphite.
Why is diamond hard?
lessons.homework: Write a 4-mark answer: 'Explain why graphite can conduct electricity but diamond cannot.'
lessons.send: SEND: model-building with sweets and sticks, labelled diagrams. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: explain why graphite is used in pencils.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: Graphene, fullerenes and nanotubes
objectives: Describe the structure of graphene, fullerenes and carbon nanotubes
Explain their properties and uses
Evaluate the benefits and risks of new carbon materials

keywords.def: a single layer of graphite, one atom thick
a hollow molecule of carbon atoms arranged in rings
a cylinder-shaped fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio
the study of structures a few nanometres in size

starter: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
Describe the structure of diamond.
State what is meant by delocalised electrons.

teach.heading: Graphene
bullets: A single layer of graphite: one atom thick
Carbon atoms in hexagons, each bonded to three others
Delocalised electrons: conducts electricity
Very strong, very light and almost transparent
teach.note: Ask: if a layer of graphite is one atom thick, what is it? Graphene. Properties arise from strong covalent bonding and delocalised electrons. Uses: electronics, composites. Mention that it was first isolated in 2004 at Manchester (Geim and Novoselov, Nobel Prize in 2010).

teach.heading: Fullerenes
bullets: Molecules of carbon forming hollow shapes
Rings of five or six carbon atoms (sometimes seven)
Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, is spherical
Bonds are strong covalent bonds
teach.note: Show a model of C60, which looks like a football. Ask pupils to say how it differs from graphite: it is a hollow cage, not a flat sheet. The first fullerene discovered was C60 in 1985. Uses: drug delivery inside the cage, lubricants, catalysts.

teach.heading: Carbon nanotubes
bullets: Cylindrical fullerenes
Very high length to diameter ratio
High tensile strength and electrical conductivity
Uses: electronics, reinforcing materials in sports equipment
teach.note: Imagine rolling up a sheet of graphene to form a tube. Ask: why are nanotubes strong? Many strong covalent bonds, along the tube. Why do they conduct? Delocalised electrons. Uses include strengthening tennis rackets and bike frames.

teach.heading: Comparing carbon structures
bullets: Diamond: 4 bonds, hard, insulator
Graphite: 3 bonds, layers, conducts
Graphene: 1 layer, conducts, strong
Fullerenes: hollow cages and tubes
teach.note: Pupils complete a table including the number of bonds per carbon atom and delocalised electrons. Ask: what do all these have in common? All are made of carbon atoms and strong covalent bonds. Their structures differ, so their properties differ. Explain that these are allotropes.

teach.heading: Benefits and risks
bullets: New materials may improve technology
Benefits: lighter and stronger materials, faster electronics
Risks: unknown long-term health and environmental effects
Scientists test new materials before wide use
teach.note: Ask pupils to weigh a proposal: use of carbon nanotubes in clothing. Benefits: strength. Risks: tiny particles could enter lungs or environment; more research needed. Practise balanced judgements. Islamic ethics encourage benefit and avoiding harm; the principle 'no harm and no reciprocating harm' (la darar wa la dirar) is a useful reflection on weighing benefit against risk.

practice: How many bonds does each carbon atom form in graphene?
Name the fullerene with 60 carbon atoms.
Why does graphene conduct electricity?
independent: Draw a diagram of graphene and label the bonds and delocalised electrons.
Explain why carbon nanotubes are used to reinforce tennis rackets. (3 marks)
Compare the structures and properties of graphene and diamond. (4 marks)
Evaluate the use of fullerenes in medicine. (4 marks)
exit: Define a fullerene.
Give one use of carbon nanotubes.
lessons.homework: Research one use of graphene or nanotubes and write a short report on the benefits and risks.
lessons.send: SEND: model-building cards, comparison table with prompts. EAL: pre-teach 'cylinder' and 'tensile'. Stretch: explain why graphene is stronger than steel per unit weight in terms of bonds.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
lessons.title: Metallic bonding, alloys and conduction
objectives: Describe metallic bonding as positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
Explain properties of metals: conductivity, malleability and high melting point
Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals

keywords.def: the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
can be hammered or bent into shape without breaking
a mixture of a metal with another element, usually another metal
electrons that are free to move in a metal

starter: Describe the structure of graphite.
Why do ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved?
Name two properties of metals.

teach.heading: Metallic bonding
bullets: Metal atoms are arranged in a regular lattice
Outer electrons are delocalised
Positive ions held by attraction to the electrons
Strong metallic bonds
teach.note: Draw a lattice of positive ions with a sea of electrons. Ask: why do metals form positive ions? They lose outer electrons. Misconception: metallic bonds are between metal atoms like covalent bonds. The attraction is between ions and delocalised electrons throughout the structure.

teach.heading: Properties of metals
bullets: High melting and boiling points: strong metallic bonds
Good conductors of electricity and heat
Malleable and ductile
Layers of ions can slide over each other
teach.note: Explain conduction: delocalised electrons carry charge, and energy, through the metal. Ask: why don't metals break when hammered like salt crystals? Layers slide but the sea of electrons keeps attracting; bonds do not break. Use a diagram to show layers sliding. Uses: electrical wiring (copper), cooking pans.

teach.heading: Alloys
bullets: A mixture of a metal and other elements
Different sized atoms distort the layers
Layers cannot slide easily
So alloys are harder than pure metals
teach.note: Draw pure metal layers and alloy layers with larger atoms. Example: pure iron is soft; steel (iron with carbon) is much harder. Brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin. Ask: why does an alloy have a different property from its parent metal? Atoms of different size block the sliding of layers.

teach.heading: Alloys in use
bullets: Steel: construction and cars
Brass: musical instruments, door fittings
Pure gold is soft: 18 carat gold is an alloy
Choose a material for the job
teach.note: Work through selecting materials: a bridge needs strong steel; a wire needs copper because it conducts. Ask: why is jewellery gold alloyed? Pure gold is too soft for rings. 24 carat is pure gold (100%) and 18 carat is 75% gold. Link to environmental issues: recycling metals saves energy and resources.

teach.heading: Linking bonding and properties
bullets: Ionic: lattice of ions, brittle, conducts when molten
Covalent small molecules: low melting point, no conduction
Giant covalent: very high melting point
Metals: conduct, malleable, high melting point
teach.note: Plenary summary of the four structures in a table. Give unknown substances with properties and ask pupils to identify the structure, e.g. 'high melting point, conducts when solid, malleable: metal'. This is a common exam question. End by reflecting on the diversity and order Allah placed in matter, a reason for gratitude and study.

practice: What type of particles carry charge in a metal?
Why are metals malleable?
Name one alloy and one of its uses.
independent: Draw a diagram of metallic bonding with labels.
Explain why copper is a good conductor of electricity. (3 marks)
Explain why steel is harder than pure iron. (3 marks)
A substance melts at 1085°C, conducts when solid and can be hammered into shape. Identify its structure and justify. (3 marks)
exit: Define alloy.
Why do metals have high melting points?
lessons.homework: Complete a summary table of ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent and metallic structures for bonding, melting point, conductivity and example.
lessons.send: SEND: structure-property matching cards. EAL: pre-teach 'malleable' and 'alloy' with objects. Stretch: explain why the conductivity of metals decreases as they get hotter (ions vibrate more, hindering electron flow).

lessons.title: Energy stores, systems and transfers
objectives: Name the energy stores and describe how energy is transferred between them
Describe energy changes in a system
State that energy is conserved and use examples of closed systems

keywords.def: an object or group of objects being studied
a way in which energy is held, such as kinetic or thermal
energy moving from one store to another
a system where no energy enters or leaves

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for electrical power.
Convert 5 kWh into joules.
Calculate the energy transferred by a 2 kW heater in 30 minutes.

teach.heading: Energy stores
bullets: Kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential
Thermal, chemical, nuclear
Magnetic and electrostatic
Energy is measured in joules (J)
teach.note: Make a list on the board and ask pupils to give an example of each store. Misconception: 'energy types' such as 'heat energy' or 'electrical energy' are used in KS3; AQA GCSE uses stores and pathways. Explain that energy is not a substance; it is a quantity we use to describe changes.

teach.heading: Energy transfers (pathways)
bullets: Mechanically: a force moving an object
Electrically: a current flowing
By heating: due to a temperature difference
By radiation: light or sound waves
teach.note: Take a kettle: electrical work from the mains transfers energy to the thermal store of the water. A moving ball hitting the ground: kinetic → thermal and sound (radiation). Ask pupils to name the transfer pathway for each. Stress that energy transferred by waves is by radiation, including sound.

teach.heading: Describing a system
bullets: Choose the system, then list the stores that change
Example: a ball thrown upwards
Kinetic store decreases; gravitational potential store increases
Energy is conserved; some is dissipated to thermal
teach.note: Build a Sankey-style list for a ball rising: kinetic → gravitational potential. For a car braking: kinetic → thermal (brakes). For a battery-powered fan: chemical → electrical → kinetic and thermal. Ask pupils to draw the energy changes as a flow diagram. Link to energy as an idea rather than something we 'use up'.

teach.heading: Closed systems
bullets: Total energy before equals total energy after
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
Energy can be transferred, stored or dissipated
In a closed system there is no net change in total energy
teach.note: Link to conservation of mass from KS3 chemistry. Ask: if energy is never destroyed, why do we say we 'run out of energy'? Because it spreads out into less useful stores, mainly thermal in the surroundings. Reflect on Qur'an 17:27 where wasteful people are brothers of the devils: we conserve useful energy sources.

teach.heading: Everyday examples
bullets: Bungee jumper: gravitational → kinetic → elastic
Swinging pendulum: GPE ↔ kinetic
Toaster: electrical → thermal and light
Phone charging: electrical → chemical
teach.note: Give each pair of pupils an example to describe in a table: starting store, final store, pathway. Check for sound as waste in many appliances. Common mistake: saying energy is 'used' or 'made' rather than transferred. Reinforce accurate language: 'transferred from ... to ...'.

practice: Name three energy stores.
What does conservation of energy mean?
How is energy transferred when a force moves an object?
independent: Describe the energy transfers in: a rollercoaster, a hairdryer, a torch, a falling apple. Use correct store names.
Draw an energy flow diagram for an electric kettle.
Explain why a bouncing ball does not return to its original height. (3 marks)
A boiling kettle loses energy to the surroundings. State where this energy goes and why it is hard to use. (2 marks)
exit: Name the pathway when a current flows.
Define closed system.
lessons.homework: Choose three appliances at home and describe the energy stores and transfers for each, with a flow diagram.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards for stores and pathways. EAL: pre-teach 'store', 'transfer', 'dissipate'. Stretch: describe the energy changes in a pendulum over one complete swing, including losses.

lessons.title: Kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy
objectives: Calculate kinetic energy using Ek = ½ m v²
Calculate gravitational potential energy using Ep = m g h
Calculate elastic potential energy using Ee = ½ k e²

keywords.def: the energy of a moving object
the energy stored by an object because of its height in a gravitational field
energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring
the force needed per metre of extension, in N/m

starter: Name the energy stores in a stretched spring.
Calculate the weight of a 4 kg mass (g = 9.8 N/kg).
State the unit of energy.

teach.heading: Kinetic energy
bullets: Ek = ½ m v²
Ek in joules, m in kg, v in m/s
Example: 1200 kg car at 20 m/s
teach.note: Model setting out: equation, substitution, answer, unit. Stress that the speed is squared before multiplying. Ask: what happens to the kinetic energy if speed doubles? It quadruples. This explains why stopping distances rise sharply with speed. Remind pupils of safe driving as a way of protecting life.

teach.heading: Gravitational potential energy
bullets: Ep = m g h
g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth
Example: 50 kg climber raised 10 m
teach.note: Check that h is vertical height. Ask: how much energy does a 0.2 kg apple gain when lifted 1.5 m? 0.2 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 2.94 J. Link to W = m g from KS3. A common error is using the length of a slope instead of the vertical height.

teach.heading: Elastic potential energy
bullets: Ee = ½ k e²
k is the spring constant in N/m
e is extension in metres
Example: k = 40 N/m, e = 0.25 m
teach.note: Calculate: Ee = ½ × 40 × 0.25² = ½ × 40 × 0.0625 = 1.25 J. Warn that extension must be in metres: 5 cm = 0.05 m. Applies as long as the spring is not stretched beyond its limit of proportionality. Ask: what is the extension? The change in length, not the total length.

teach.heading: Energy changes in motion
bullets: Falling object: Ep → Ek (ignoring air resistance)
Ek gained = Ep lost
Find speed: v² = 2 × Ek ÷ m
Example: 2 kg falls 5 m: Ep = 98 J
teach.note: Calculate the final speed of a 2 kg ball dropped from 5 m: Ek = 98 J, so v² = 2 × 98 ÷ 2 = 98, v ≈ 9.9 m/s. Good for higher-attaining pupils. Ask: does the mass change the speed? No, it cancels. Mention air resistance would reduce the speed.

teach.heading: Choosing the right equation
bullets: Moving? Use Ek
Lifted up? Use Ep
Stretched or compressed? Use Ee
Write the equation, substitute, calculate, give the unit
teach.note: Give a mixed set of statements and pupils choose. Mini-whiteboard quick fire. Remind pupils that in the AQA exam they must recall the Ek and Ep equations, while the Ee equation and ΔE = m c Δθ are given on the equation sheet. The value of g is given in questions. Practise units and rounding to two or three significant figures.

practice: Calculate Ek of a 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s.
State the unit of the spring constant.
What happens to Ek if the speed doubles?
independent: Calculate Ek of a 70 kg runner at 8 m/s.
Calculate Ep gained by a 12 kg box raised 3 m (g = 9.8 N/kg).
A spring with k = 80 N/m is stretched by 6 cm. Calculate the energy stored.
A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from 20 m. Calculate its Ep and its speed just before hitting the ground (ignoring air resistance).
exit: Write the equation for kinetic energy.
Calculate Ep for a 2 kg mass raised 5 m (g = 9.8 N/kg).
lessons.homework: Calculate your own gravitational potential energy gain when you climb a flight of stairs (estimate mass and height).
lessons.send: SEND: equation cards with example layouts. EAL: pre-teach 'extension' and 'kinetic'. Stretch: derive the speed of a falling object from energy conservation and compare with v² = 2gh.

lessons.title: Specific heat capacity and the required practical
objectives: Define specific heat capacity and use ΔE = m c Δθ
Describe the required practical to determine the specific heat capacity of a solid or liquid
Evaluate the sources of error in the practical

keywords.def: the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C
energy held in the motion and arrangement of particles
an electrical heater placed in a liquid or in a block
material used to reduce energy transferred by heating

starter: Write the equation for energy transferred by a heater.
Calculate the energy transferred by a 60 W heater in 5 minutes.
State the unit of power.

teach.heading: What is specific heat capacity?
bullets: The energy needed to heat 1 kg by 1°C
Different materials need different energies
Water has a high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C)
Units: J/kg°C
teach.note: Ask: why does a sandy beach get hot while the sea stays cool? Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it takes more energy to heat. Compare water (4200), aluminium (900), copper (390). Misconception: specific heat capacity is the same as temperature. It measures how hard it is to change the temperature.

teach.heading: The equation
bullets: ΔE = m c Δθ
ΔE: change in thermal energy (J)
m: mass (kg); c: SHC (J/kg°C)
Δθ: temperature change (°C)
teach.note: Worked example: raise 0.5 kg of water by 20°C. ΔE = 0.5 × 4200 × 20 = 42 000 J. Rearrange to find Δθ or c. Ask: how long would a 2000 W kettle take? 42 000 ÷ 2000 = 21 s (ideal). Emphasise that mass must be in kilograms.

teach.heading: Required practical: the method
bullets: Weigh a 1 kg aluminium block
Insert an immersion heater and thermometer; add insulation
Record the starting temperature
Heat for 10 minutes; record the voltage and current; record temperature every minute
teach.note: Show a video or diagram. Energy supplied = p.d. × current × time (E = V I t). Example: 12 V, 5 A for 600 s gives 36 000 J. Use oil in the thermometer hole to improve thermal contact. Safety: hot surfaces and electricity near water. Note that this practical cannot be done safely at home; use data from the video or the teacher demonstration.

teach.heading: Calculating c
bullets: Energy supplied: 12 × 5 × 600 = 36 000 J
Temperature rise: 38°C (20°C to 58°C)
c ≈ 950 J/kg°C
teach.note: The accepted value for aluminium is 900 J/kg°C; the result is a little higher because some energy was transferred to the surroundings, so not all the energy supplied heated the block. Calculate the percentage difference. Plot temperature against time: a straight line suggests a constant rate of heating. Use the gradient to find c: c = P ÷ (m × gradient).

teach.heading: Improving the investigation
bullets: Insulate the block with foam or cotton wool
Use a lid for water in a beaker
Stir liquids for even temperature
Use a more precise thermometer; repeat
teach.note: Discuss sources of error: heat loss, thermometer lag, poor thermal contact, heater not fully inside the block. Ask: why does insulation make the result closer to the true value? Less energy is dissipated. Qur'an 7:31 encourages us not to be wasteful; link to reducing waste in heating.

practice: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
Calculate the energy to heat 2 kg of water by 5°C (c = 4200 J/kg°C).
Why is insulation used in the practical?
independent: Calculate the energy needed to heat 3 kg of aluminium from 20°C to 60°C (c = 900 J/kg°C).
A 2 kW kettle heats 1.5 kg of water from 20°C to 100°C. Calculate the energy needed, and the time taken in an ideal case.
A copper block of mass 0.8 kg is heated with 15 000 J and rises by 48°C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.
Explain why the experimental value of c is usually higher than the accepted value. (3 marks)
exit: Write the equation linking energy, mass, SHC and temperature change.
Name one way to improve the accuracy of the practical.
lessons.homework: Write a method for determining the specific heat capacity of a metal block, with a labelled diagram and two safety points.
lessons.send: SEND: equation triangle with units; worked example frame. EAL: key terms with diagrams. Stretch: use a temperature-time graph gradient to find c.

lessons.title: Conservation of energy and efficiency
objectives: Explain energy dissipation and wasted energy
Calculate efficiency as a ratio or percentage
Suggest ways of increasing the efficiency of a device

keywords.def: spread out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy
energy transferred to the store we want
the proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred
energy transferred to stores that are not useful

starter: State the law of conservation of energy.
Name the energy stores involved when a kettle boils water.
Convert 36 000 J into kJ.

teach.heading: Wasted energy
bullets: Not all energy is transferred usefully
Wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings
Usually transferred to the thermal store by heating
Total energy is still conserved
teach.note: Take a light bulb: electrical → light (useful), thermal (wasted). A filament bulb transfers about 5-10% usefully. Ask: where does the wasted energy end up? Surroundings, warming the air. It cannot be used again easily. Misconception: wasted energy has disappeared.

teach.heading: Efficiency
bullets: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input
Give as a decimal or a percentage
Never more than 100%
Efficiency has no units
teach.note: Equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer; or with power. Example: a motor takes in 500 J and gives 350 J of useful kinetic energy: 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70 or 70%. Wasted energy = 150 J. Ask: can efficiency be 110%? No, as it would break conservation of energy.

teach.heading: Efficiency calculations
bullets: A lamp: input 100 J, useful light 8 J → 8%
An LED: input 10 J, light 3 J → 30%
Wasted = input − useful
Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
teach.note: Include a power version: an LED lamp with input 8 W gives 2 W of light: 25%. Practise rearranging to find useful output: 40% of 2000 J = 800 J. Link to the electricity topic: more efficient lamps save money and reduce waste, an application of avoiding israf.

teach.heading: Sankey diagrams
bullets: Arrow width shows the energy
Useful output continues straight
Wasted energy branches off
Total input = useful + wasted
teach.note: Draw a Sankey diagram for a motor on the board: 500 J in, 350 J useful, 150 J wasted as heat and sound. Use a scale such as 1 mm = 10 J. Sankey diagrams are not required by AQA but help pupils see that energy is conserved. Ask pupils to draw one for a kettle.

teach.heading: Increasing efficiency
bullets: Lubricate moving parts to reduce friction
Use streamlined shapes to reduce drag
Insulate to reduce heat loss
Use components that waste less energy
teach.note: Ask pupils how the efficiency of a bicycle can be increased: oil the chain, pump the tyres, use a streamlined posture. Link back to friction. Discuss why a 100% efficient device is impossible. Pupils then evaluate cost versus benefit of upgrading an appliance.

practice: Define wasted energy.
Calculate the efficiency of a device with 200 J input and 50 J useful output.
Can efficiency be greater than 100%? Explain.
independent: A motor takes in 800 J and wastes 200 J. Calculate the useful energy and the efficiency.
A lamp has an efficiency of 15% and is supplied with 600 J. Calculate the useful energy transferred.
An LED lamp is 25% efficient and a filament lamp is 5% efficient. Each is supplied with 200 J. Calculate the useful light and the wasted energy for each, and state which is better. (4 marks)
Suggest three ways to increase the efficiency of a bicycle. (3 marks)
exit: Write the equation for efficiency.
Where does most wasted energy end up?
lessons.homework: Find the energy rating or efficiency of two household appliances and compare their running costs and efficiency.
lessons.send: SEND: efficiency formula triangle; worked example. EAL: pre-teach 'dissipated' and 'efficient'. Stretch: explain why efficiency can never be 100% in a real device, referring to friction and heating.

lessons.title: Power and reducing unwanted energy transfers
objectives: Calculate power as the rate of energy transfer, P = E ÷ t and P = W ÷ t
Explain how thermal conductivity affects the rate of cooling
Explain how lubrication and insulation reduce unwanted transfers

keywords.def: the rate at which energy is transferred, in watts
one joule per second
a measure of how well a material transfers energy by conduction
using oil or grease to reduce friction between moving surfaces

starter: Calculate the efficiency of a device with 400 J input and 300 J useful output.
State the unit of energy and the unit of power.
Define wasted energy.

teach.heading: Power
bullets: Power = energy transferred ÷ time
P = E ÷ t; also P = W ÷ t (work done)
1 watt = 1 joule per second
Example: crane lifts 58 800 J in 20 s: 2940 W
teach.note: Two machines can do the same job but at different rates: a more powerful machine transfers energy faster. Example: a 500 kg load lifted 12 m: E = 500 × 9.8 × 12 = 58 800 J. If it takes 20 s, P = 2940 W. If it takes 10 s, P = 5880 W. Ask: which machine is more powerful? The one that does it in less time. Common error: using minutes.

teach.heading: Comparing power
bullets: Two students run up the same stairs
Same energy gained, different times
Quicker means higher power
Power ratings on appliances show the rate of use
teach.note: Calculate: a 60 kg student climbs stairs 4 m high. Ep = 60 × 9.8 × 4 = 2352 J. In 8 s, P = 294 W; in 6 s, P = 392 W. Ask pupils to explain why both gain the same energy but different power. Link to kWh from electricity: kWh is power × time.

teach.heading: Conduction and thermal conductivity
bullets: Conduction: energy passes through a material as particles vibrate
Metals have high thermal conductivity
Insulators such as wool and plastic have low values
Rate of energy transfer depends on the thermal conductivity and thickness
teach.note: Include the effect on a house: thicker walls with lower thermal conductivity reduce the rate of heat loss. Experiment (video): metal rods coated in wax on a heat source; wax melts at different rates. Ask: why are saucepan handles plastic? They are poor conductors.

teach.heading: Reducing heat loss in the home
bullets: Loft insulation, cavity wall insulation
Double glazing and draught excluders
Low thermal conductivity materials trap air
Thicker walls lose energy more slowly
teach.note: Discuss payback time: if loft insulation costs £400 and saves £100 per year, payback is 4 years. Ask pupils to evaluate the options. Note the link with Qur'an 7:31 where wastefulness is discouraged, and the benefit of saving money for essential needs.

teach.heading: Friction and lubrication
bullets: Friction between moving parts transfers energy to thermal stores
Lubricants (oil, grease) reduce friction
Bearings reduce friction in wheels
Reduces wear and wasted energy
teach.note: Ask: why does an engine need oil? To reduce friction and wear, and so improve efficiency. Discuss a bike chain: cleaning and oiling. Link to efficiency in the last lesson. Close by emphasising: reducing unwanted energy transfers increases efficiency.

practice: State the unit of power.
Calculate the power of a machine that transfers 1500 J in 30 s.
Why are saucepan handles made of plastic?
independent: A motor lifts a 40 kg load by 5 m in 10 s. Calculate the useful energy gained and the power. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
Compare two students climbing the same stairs: one in 5 s, the other in 8 s. Who has the larger power? Explain.
Explain how cavity wall insulation reduces energy loss from a house. (3 marks)
Loft insulation costs £450 and saves £90 per year. Calculate the payback time and suggest whether it is worthwhile. (3 marks)
exit: Write the equation linking power, energy and time.
State one way to reduce friction in a machine.
lessons.homework: Walk up a flight of stairs at home, time yourself, estimate mass and height, and calculate your power.
lessons.send: SEND: step-by-step power calculation frame. EAL: pre-teach 'rate' and 'insulate'. Stretch: explain why two materials of the same thickness can lose heat at different rates in terms of particles.

lessons.title: Energy resources
objectives: Distinguish renewable from non-renewable energy resources
Describe the main energy resources used for transport, electricity generation and heating
Evaluate the reliability, cost and environmental effects of different resources

keywords.def: a resource that is replenished as it is used
a resource that will run out because it cannot be replaced quickly
coal, oil or gas formed from the remains of living things over millions of years
a fuel made from plant or animal material

starter: State the energy change in a power station.
Define efficiency.
Name two fossil fuels.

teach.heading: Non-renewable resources
bullets: Fossil fuels: coal, oil, natural gas
Nuclear fuel: uranium and plutonium
Will eventually run out
Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned
teach.note: Link to the carbon cycle and climate change from Year 8. Ask: why does burning fossil fuels increase carbon dioxide? Carbon stored for millions of years is released. Nuclear power does not release CO2 when running but makes radioactive waste. Fossil fuels are used for transport, heating and generation.

teach.heading: Renewable resources
bullets: Wind, solar, hydroelectric, tides, waves
Geothermal, biofuels
Do not run out
Many have no carbon dioxide emissions in use
teach.note: Make a list with examples. Pupils sort each as electricity, heating or transport. Biofuels can be used for transport and electricity; solar can heat water or generate electricity with cells. Ask: how does a wind turbine work? Kinetic energy of wind turns a generator. Qur'an 30:41 can prompt discussion of the environment and human responsibility.

teach.heading: Reliability
bullets: Wind and solar depend on weather and daylight
Tidal is predictable; waves vary
Hydroelectric and geothermal are reliable
Fossil fuel and nuclear can run continuously
teach.note: Present a day's demand curve and ask pupils how the grid copes when wind is low. Discuss energy storage, such as pumped storage hydroelectric, and a mix of resources. Misconception: renewable means unreliable; it depends on the type. Compare start-up times: gas stations start quickly, nuclear slowly.

teach.heading: Costs and environmental impact
bullets: Capital cost, running cost and decommissioning
Wind: visual and noise impact, bird deaths
Hydroelectric: floods habitats
Nuclear: radioactive waste; fossil fuels: CO₂ and acid rain
teach.note: Complete a table: resource, advantages, disadvantages. Ask: which resource is best for an island community? Encourage justified answers with trade-offs. Mention that decisions involve economic, social and environmental factors, not only science.

teach.heading: Trends and evaluating
bullets: Use of renewables is increasing in the UK
Reasons: climate targets, falling costs, government policy
Obstacles: cost, reliability, public opinion
Write balanced answers with a conclusion
teach.note: Present a table of the percentage of UK electricity from different sources over several years (use the latest UK government energy statistics). Ask pupils to describe trends. Model a 6-mark evaluation: advantages, disadvantages, conclusion. Close with gratitude for the resources Allah has provided and our duty to use them responsibly.

practice: Give two renewable resources.
Why do fossil fuels contribute to climate change?
Which renewable resource is predictable every day?
independent: Complete a table of eight energy resources: renewable or not, advantages, disadvantages.
Explain why solar cells are not suitable as the only source of electricity in the UK. (3 marks)
Evaluate the use of nuclear power for electricity generation. (4 marks)
A town is considering building a wind farm. Give two arguments for and two against. (4 marks)
exit: Define renewable resource.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of hydroelectric power.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Evaluate the use of renewable energy resources to generate electricity in the UK.'
lessons.send: SEND: table template with prompts; picture cards. EAL: glossary for 'renewable', 'reliable' and 'emissions'. Stretch: analyse data on UK energy mix and suggest how the grid could meet demand on a still night.
